title: React Server Components
subtitle: React for two computers
throughline: One render crossing the network: a Server Component tree turned into a Flight stream, rebuilt on the client, then a Server Action call sent back the other way.

chapters.title: Two Computers, One Tree
chapters.blurb: The core idea behind Server Components: a single React tree split across a server and a browser, joined by a serialization boundary.

steps.title: Two Computers, One Tree
steps.narration: **React Server Components** let one component tree span two machines. We'll follow the protocol React calls **Flight**, from the spec up — not any one framework's wiring.
steps.say: React Server Components ask a strange question. What if one component tree could run on two computers at once? Let's follow the protocol that makes it work, the one React calls Flight.

steps.title: A tree split in two
steps.narration: Some components are **Server Components** — they run once, on the server, and their code never reaches the browser. Others are **Client Components**, whose code ships down to run in the page.
steps.say: In a normal app, every component runs in the browser. Server Components change that. Some components run once, on the server, and their code never ships. Others are client components, and only those reach the browser.

steps.title: Render to a description
steps.narration: On the server, **`ReactFlightServer`** renders the tree — but instead of HTML, it produces a *description* of the rendered output: elements, props, and plain values.
steps.say: On the server, the Flight Server renders the tree. But it doesn't produce HTML. It produces a description of what was rendered: the elements, their props, and the plain values inside them.

steps.title: A stream of rows
steps.narration: That description is serialized into a **stream of numbered rows** and flushed to the client as it becomes ready — not as one finished blob.
steps.say: That description is serialized into a stream of numbered rows. Each row is written and flushed as soon as it's ready, so the page can start filling in before the server has finished.

steps.title: The client rebuilds the tree
steps.narration: On the other computer, **`ReactFlightClient`** reads those rows and reconstructs the very same React tree — without ever running the Server Component's code.
steps.say: On the other computer, the Flight Client reads those rows back and rebuilds the very same tree. It never runs the server component's code. It just receives the result of having run it.

steps.title: Code only where it runs
steps.narration: Where the tree hits a **Client Component**, the stream carries a *reference*, not code — and the client loads that module to make it interactive.
steps.say: Where the tree meets a client component, the stream doesn't carry its code. It carries a reference to it. The client loads that module separately, so interactive code lives only in the browser, and server code stays on the server.

steps.title: One tree, two machines
steps.narration: So the whole journey is: render on the server, serialize to a stream, rebuild on the client, and load client code only where it's needed. The rest of the book opens each of these boxes.
steps.say: So that's the shape of it. Render on the server, serialize to a stream, rebuild on the client, and load browser code only where it's truly needed. Now let's open each of these boxes in turn.

chapters.title: The Flight Stream
chapters.blurb: How the server turns a React tree into a stream of numbered rows — the wire format at the heart of Flight.

nodes.label: outlineModel
nodes.sublabel: shared value to its own row

steps.title: The Flight Stream
steps.narration: Flight's wire format is deliberately humble: a sequence of **numbered rows**, each a tiny header plus JSON. Let's watch the server build one.
steps.say: The Flight wire format is deliberately humble. It's just a sequence of numbered rows, each one a tiny header followed by some JSON. Let's watch the server build that stream.

steps.title: Walking the tree
steps.narration: **`renderModelDestructive`** walks the rendered model value by value — elements, arrays, objects, and primitives — deciding how each one crosses the wire.
steps.say: Serialization starts with a function called render model destructive. It walks the rendered tree value by value: each element, each array, each object, each primitive, deciding how that piece should cross the wire.

steps.title: Every row gets a number
steps.narration: A counter, **`nextChunkId`**, hands out an id per row. The header is just that id and a one-letter tag — `serializeRowHeader` writes `id` then `tag`.
steps.say: Every row gets a number from a counter called next chunk id. The header couldn't be simpler: the row's number, then a single letter tag that says what kind of row this is.

steps.title: Header, then JSON
steps.narration: **`emitModelChunk`** writes a model row: the numeric header, then the value as JSON, then a newline. A simple object becomes one self-describing line in the stream.
steps.say: Emit model chunk writes the row itself: the numbered header, then the value as ordinary JSON, then a newline. A plain object becomes one self-describing line in the stream.

steps.title: References, not copies
steps.narration: Special values get escaped with a `$` prefix: a plain reference to another row is `$` plus its id, and `$L` marks a *lazy* one React can suspend on. `serializeByValueID` and `serializeLazyID` write these.
steps.say: Not everything is plain JSON. Special values are escaped with a dollar sign. A reference to another row is a dollar sign and that row's number. A lazy reference adds an L, marking a value React can suspend on until it arrives.

steps.title: Big or shared values move out
steps.narration: **`outlineModel`** pulls a shared or large value into *its own* numbered row and leaves a reference behind — so it's sent once and pointed at from many places.
steps.say: When a value is large or shared in several places, outline model lifts it into its very own numbered row and leaves a reference where it used to be. That way it travels once, and everything else just points at it.

steps.title: A stream, not a snapshot
steps.narration: Because rows are flushed as they're ready, a slow value can arrive *later* as a new row referencing the same id — the client doesn't wait for the whole tree.
steps.say: And because rows flush the moment they're ready, a slow part of the tree can show up later as a new row pointing at the same number. The client never has to wait for the whole tree to finish.

steps.title: From tree to wire
steps.narration: So serialization is: walk the model, number each row, escape references with `$`, outline shared values, and flush — a stream of self-describing lines.
steps.say: So the whole serializer is just that: walk the model, number each row, escape references with a dollar sign, outline the shared values, and flush. What comes out is a stream of self-describing lines.

chapters.title: Client References
chapters.blurb: How a Server Component points at code it can't run — and the client loads that module by name.

steps.title: Client References
steps.narration: A Server Component can *use* a Client Component without running it. The trick is a **client reference** — a name the browser can resolve to real code.
steps.say: Here's the puzzle at the center of Server Components. The server renders a tree that includes interactive parts it must not run. How? It points at them by name. Let's follow one of those pointers.
steps.coverSubtitle: Pointing at code you can't run

steps.title: The server can't run this
steps.narration: When the render reaches a **Client Component**, the server holds only a **client reference** — a marker tagging which module and export it is, with no executable body.
steps.say: When the server's render reaches a client component, it doesn't have its code to run. All it holds is a client reference: a marker that records which module this is and which export, but nothing it can execute.

steps.title: Look it up in the manifest
steps.narration: **`resolveClientReferenceMetadata`** looks the reference up in **`bundlerConfig`**, the client manifest, to learn the module id, its chunks, and the export name the browser will need.
steps.say: To turn that marker into something the browser can use, React looks it up in the bundler config, the client manifest. That lookup yields the module's id, the chunks it lives in, and the name of the export to grab.

steps.title: Emit an import row
steps.narration: That metadata becomes an **`I` row** in the stream, and where the component sat, the tree gets a `$L` *lazy reference* pointing at it — code and placeholder, sent separately.
steps.say: The metadata is written into the stream as its own row, tagged with the letter I for import. And where the component used to be, the tree holds a lazy reference pointing at that import row. The placeholder and the code travel apart.

steps.title: The client reads the metadata
steps.narration: On the browser, **`resolveModule`** receives that import row and prepares to fetch the module the metadata names.
steps.say: On the browser, a function called resolve module receives that import row. It reads the metadata and gets ready to fetch exactly the module it names. No more, no less.

steps.title: Load the real module
steps.narration: **`requireModule`** then loads the actual client code and pulls out the named export — now there's a real, runnable **Client Component** in the browser.
steps.say: Then require module does the real work. It loads the client code and pulls out the named export. For the first time in this whole journey, there is a genuine, runnable component sitting in the browser.

steps.title: Suspend until it lands
steps.narration: Until that module loads, the `$L` lazy reference is a **`createLazyChunkWrapper`** React can suspend on — so the tree renders the moment the code is ready, and not before.
steps.say: And what about that lazy reference back in the tree? React wraps it so it can suspend on it, just like any other lazy value. The surrounding tree renders the instant the code is ready, and waits patiently until then.

steps.title: Code loaded by name
steps.narration: Reference in the manifest, `I` row on the wire, `resolveModule` and `requireModule` on the client: that's how interactive code crosses without the server ever running it.
steps.say: So that's the boundary between the two computers, made concrete. A reference in the manifest, an import row on the wire, resolve and require on the client. Interactive code crosses over, and the server never runs a line of it.

chapters.title: Rebuilding the Tree
chapters.blurb: On the client, rows become chunks with a lifecycle — and unresolved chunks let React suspend until the rest of the stream arrives.

steps.title: Rebuilding the Tree
steps.narration: The client turns the byte stream into **chunks** — small promises with a lifecycle — and assembles them into a React tree that can render before the stream ends.
steps.say: Now to the receiving end. The client turns the incoming bytes into chunks, little promises with a lifecycle, and weaves them into a React tree that can start rendering long before the stream is done.

steps.title: Bytes become rows
steps.narration: **`processBinaryChunk`** is a tiny state machine: it reads the row id, then the one-letter tag, then the row body up to a newline — slicing the stream back into rows.
steps.say: Process binary chunk is a tiny state machine. It reads the row's number, then its one letter tag, then the body up to a newline. Byte by byte, it slices the flat stream back into the rows the server wrote.

steps.title: Each row is a chunk
steps.narration: Each id maps to a **chunk** in a map — a `ReactPromise` that moves through states: `pending`, then `resolved_model`, then `fulfilled` once its value is built.
steps.say: Each numbered row becomes a chunk in a map, keyed by its id. A chunk is really a promise that walks through states: pending at first, then resolved model once its text arrives, then fulfilled once its value is fully built.

steps.title: Decoding the markers
steps.narration: When a chunk initializes, **`parseModelString`** walks its JSON and decodes every `$` marker: a reference becomes the chunk it names, a symbol, a date, a bigint — each rebuilt.
steps.say: When a chunk initializes, parse model string walks its JSON looking for those dollar sign markers. A reference turns back into the chunk it names. A symbol, a date, a big integer, each is rebuilt into the real value it stood for.

steps.title: A reference becomes a value
steps.narration: For a reference, **`getChunk`** fetches the target by id. If it hasn't arrived, that's a **pending chunk** — a hole the tree is allowed to wait on.
steps.say: When parse model string meets a reference, it calls get chunk to fetch the target by its number. Sometimes that target hasn't streamed in yet. Then it's a pending chunk: a hole in the tree that React is allowed to wait on.

steps.title: Suspend on what's missing
steps.narration: A pending chunk is wrapped so React can **suspend** on it. The finished parts of the **React tree** render now; the gap shows a fallback until its row lands.
steps.say: Because a pending chunk is just a promise, React can suspend on it. The parts of the tree that are ready render immediately. Wherever a value is still missing, React shows a fallback and simply waits.

steps.title: Resolve, and fill the gap
steps.narration: When the awaited row finally arrives, **`resolveModelChunk`** flips it to `fulfilled`, every chunk waiting on it wakes, and that part of the tree quietly fills in.
steps.say: Then the awaited row finally arrives. Resolving it flips the chunk to fulfilled, and every chunk that was blocked on it wakes up. The fallback disappears, and that branch of the tree fills itself in, all on its own.

steps.title: A tree that streams itself in
steps.narration: Rows to chunks, markers decoded by `parseModelString`, missing values suspended on, then resolved: the tree assembles progressively, never blocking on the slowest branch.
steps.say: So the client side is the mirror of the server. Rows become chunks, markers get decoded, missing values are suspended on, and as the stream catches up, they resolve. The tree assembles itself progressively, never held hostage by its slowest branch.

chapters.title: Server Actions
chapters.blurb: The reply path: a client holds a handle to a server function, calls it, and React serializes the arguments back across the wire to run it.

steps.title: Server Actions
steps.narration: So far data flowed server to client. **Server Actions** — the functions behind `useActionState` and form actions — run the other way: the client invokes code that lives on the server.
steps.say: Everything so far has flowed from server to client. Server Actions run the other direction. They're the functions behind form actions and use action state, and they let the browser call code that only ever lives on the server.
steps.coverSubtitle: A call back across the wire

steps.title: A handle, not the function
steps.narration: On the client, **`createServerReference`** returns a stand-in function. Calling it doesn't run anything locally — it calls **`callServer`** with the action's id and the arguments.
steps.say: On the client, what looks like a normal async function is really a stand-in built by create server reference. Calling it runs nothing locally. Instead it hands the action's id and your arguments to a callback named call server.

steps.title: Encode the arguments
steps.narration: **`processReply`** serializes the arguments — the same `$` escapes as Flight, in reverse — into a reply, ready to send.
steps.say: To send those arguments, React runs process reply. It serializes them using the very same dollar sign escapes as the Flight stream, just in the opposite direction, turning your arguments into something that can travel.

steps.title: Arguments become a reply
steps.narration: The result is **`FormData`**: plain args as fields, and the action itself tagged with `$ACTION_ID_` or, when it has bound arguments, `$ACTION_REF_`.
steps.say: What comes out is form data. The plain arguments become ordinary fields, and the action itself is tagged with a special action id field. If the action carries bound arguments, those ride along under an action reference field instead.

steps.title: Send it to the server
steps.narration: The reply is POSTed back. On the server, **`decodeAction`** scans the form for the `$ACTION_` fields and pulls the rest aside as the real arguments.
steps.say: The reply is posted back to the server. There, decode action scans the form data for those action fields, sets the implementation details aside, and keeps the rest as the actual arguments to the call.

steps.title: Find the real function
steps.narration: **`resolveServerReference`** looks the id up in the **`ServerManifest`** — the mirror of the client manifest — to find the module that actually holds the function.
steps.say: Now the server has an id but not a function. Resolve server reference looks that id up in the server manifest, the mirror image of the client manifest, and finds the module that genuinely contains the code to run.

steps.title: Bind the args, run it
steps.narration: **`loadServerReference`** preloads the module, **`bindArgs`** binds any bound arguments, and the **Server Function** finally runs — back on the machine that owns it.
steps.say: With the module in hand, load server reference makes sure it's loaded, bind args attaches any bound arguments, and at last the server function runs, on the one machine that was ever allowed to run it.

steps.title: The answer streams back
steps.narration: The function's return value is re-serialized as a **Flight response** to the same client — closing the loop, and `decodeFormState` can carry form state along for `useActionState`.
steps.say: And the result? It's serialized right back as a Flight response to the same client, in the very format we started with. The loop is closed. For forms, the server can even thread the new state back, which is what powers use action state.

chapters.title: The Whole Round Trip
chapters.blurb: Tracing one render and one action across both computers — and the temporary references that let opaque values survive the journey.

steps.title: The Whole Round Trip
steps.narration: Let's trace the whole loop end to end — render down, action up — and meet the **temporary references** that let opaque values cross and come home unchanged.
steps.say: Let's put it all together and trace the whole loop end to end. Render flowing down, an action flowing back up, and one last trick that lets values cross over and come home unchanged.

steps.title: Down: server to client
steps.narration: A **Server Component** renders to the **Flight stream**, and the **Flight Client** rebuilds that exact tree in the browser — the path from chapters two through four.
steps.say: The trip down is everything we've seen. A server component renders into the Flight stream as numbered rows, and the Flight client reads them back to rebuild that exact tree in the browser.

steps.title: Mount the interactive parts
steps.narration: Among the rebuilt tree sits a **Server Action** — a client-side handle, created by `createServerReference`, to a function that lives on the server.
steps.say: Woven into that rebuilt tree is a server action: a small handle on the client that stands in for a function back on the server, waiting for someone to call it.

steps.title: Up: client to server
steps.narration: Invoking it runs the reply path: arguments encoded into a **FormData reply** and POSTed to the **Server Function**, which resolves and runs — the path from chapter five.
steps.say: When you invoke it, the reply path runs in reverse. The arguments are encoded into a form data reply, posted back, and the matching server function is resolved and run.

steps.title: Opaque values round-trip
steps.narration: Some values can't be serialized. A **temporary reference** (`$T`) stands in for them — held in a set so a value sent client to server and back arrives as the *same* object.
steps.say: But what about values that can't be serialized at all? React assigns them a temporary reference, an opaque token held in a set on each side. A value sent over and handed back comes home as the very same object, never copied, just remembered.

steps.title: Answered in the same language
steps.narration: The function's result is re-serialized into a fresh **Flight stream** back to the client — the same protocol in both directions, closing the loop.
steps.say: And the server answers in the same language it spoke before. The function's result is serialized into a fresh Flight stream and sent back, the one protocol carrying every leg of the journey.

steps.title: React for two computers
steps.narration: One tree, one protocol, two machines: render down as rows, hydrate and interact, call back up, run, and answer — Flight is the seam that makes it feel like one app.
steps.say: That's React Server Components, from principles. One tree, one protocol, two computers. Render flows down as rows, the page comes alive, an action calls back up, the server runs it and answers. Flight is the seam that makes two machines feel like a single app.
